newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria urges OPEC to freeze output quotas.
newsitem.headline: Algeria urges OPEC to freeze output quotas.

text.p: Algeria's energy minister urged his OPEC colleagues, who meet in Vienna this week, to freeze current output quotas.
"The current OPEC output ceiling of 25.03 million barrel per day should not be increased," said Amar Makloufi in remarks quoted on Tuesday by the Algerian government-controlled newspaper al Chaab.
Makhloufi, who was quoted by the newspaper as speaking at the fringe of a two-day conference over Algeria's energy prospects held in Algiers, added:
"There is a consensus among OPEC to uphold the current (output) ceiling since the prices are sound".
An average of almost $20 per barrel so far this year is up $3 from 1995 and is the firmest since the Gulf war in 1991.
The higher prices added up to a windfall extra $30 billion in revenues for OPEC exporters whose economies were crimped in recent years when oil prices languished in the bargain basement.

Makhloufi, who did not comment on the possible early resumption of sales by Iraq, said "raising the ceiling is not in the interest of OPEC's country members and it is preferable for the market that OPEC renews the ceiling to reach a better price."
OPEC, which begins its twice-yearly conference on Wednesday in Vienna had already pencilled a return of Iraqi oil to its production quota system when it last met in June.

Iraq's ambassador at the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, said on Monday that Baghdad had agreed to all U.N. conditions that had held up implementing an oil-for-food accord designed to ease the 1991 Gulf War embargo on Iraqi oil exports.

OPEC's thorniest problem is that several of the 11 group members are cheating on their assigned supply quotas, and total OPEC daily volumes is already almost a million barrels above the intended ceiling of 25.03 million, even before the Iraqi crude flows to the international market.
"Algeria has not passed its quota of 750,000 barrel per day," said Makhloufi urging other OPEC members to respect their assigned quotas.
